 Sioux Falls graduates trail the state in seeking education after high school — this effort aims to close the gap
 Jodi Schwan 
 8 hours ago 
 Share 
 Tweet 
 LinkedIn 
 Oct. 29, 2026 
 Since when is applying for federal student aid for college a party?
 Well, maybe it’s getting closer — as each of the four high schools in the Sioux Falls School Distirct hosted a “Financial Aid Fiesta” in October — the month when the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or FAFSA, is released by the U.S. Department of Education.
 It’s one of many new efforts brought to the school district this year with the expansion of the nonprofit Promising Futures College & Career Access program. Last year, it began as a pilot program at Jefferson High School, and this year, 12 college and career advisers are placed across the four high schools, funded by a more than $1 million donation from The Promising Futures Fund to the school district.
 “No. 1, it’s about helping kids find a path out of poverty,” said Steve Hildebrand, founder of Promising Futures. “The No. 2 goal is helping our community with workforce.”
 The data suggests there is plenty of opportunity.
 For the class of 2025, 54 percent of Sioux Falls School District graduates were enrolled in postsecondary education at any time during the first year after graduation, while the state average was 59 percent.
 For the class of 2024, two years’ post-graduation, 61 percent of Sioux Falls graduates were enrolled in postsecondary education, compared with a statewide average of 64 percent.
 “We knew when we were putting the program together that financial barriers were going to be the largest issue we had to deal with,” Hildebrand said. “It’s the No. 1 reason students don’t go to college or technical school.”
 Promising Futures advisers spend about half their time helping navigate financial barriers, he said.
 At the “fiesta,” parents and students enjoyed a free meal. But the real recipe is for the students’ futures. It’s a chance to discuss financial aid and complete the FAFSA — something the career counselors have been helping with since the beginning of the month.
 “The months of October and November provide an opportunity for students to apply to any South Dakota public university for free – application fees are waived,” Hildebrand said.
 “We are using this as an opportunity to encourage students to get applications in early. We have a big push going on in all four public high schools.”
 Filling out a FAFSA “is not fun,” he acknowledges. “Wealthy families don’t like to do it, let alone low-income families who have a lot more barriers. And in our school district, because we’ve been an immigrant-welcoming community, there are so many different immigration statuses for our team to learn all the ways to navigate an application for federal student aid. It was a challenge. But we know so much more now.”
 The program builds on Promising Futures’ years of success with college visits and related experiences for eighth graders and some high school students.  In addition to visiting universities in South Dakota, there will be college and community visits for students involved in volleyball, wrestling, soccer, football, theater and orchestra by the end of the year.
 The impact even in the pilot year at Jefferson was noticeable, said Dan Conrad, assistant superintendent for the school district.
 “The first year was positive,” he said. “Steve’s persistence to rally the troops in the community behind a common cause is the inspiring part. Our goal is to help kids have an idea or an opportunity and remove any barriers we can, so if they want to, they can go to school and continue their education through a two-year or four-year degree or a career.”
 The advisers supplement the work of existing school counselors, who often work with as many as 350 to 400 students each on a range of issues beyond college and career guidance.
 “It’s hard to go into the depth that sometimes is required to help kids find financial opportunities,” Conrad said. “They (the advisers) are there to help dig through whatever the barrier might be and find an opportunity to help the student access college.”
 This fall, the expanded team got off to a fast start.
 Advisers also hosted a first lunch-and-learn event for the year, inviting teams from Avera Health and Sanford Health to come in to talk to students about Avera Academy and Sanford Classrooms to Careers – both ways that student can attain credits while in high school.
 “They are also hosting lunch-and-learns bringing in medical personnel to discuss careers in medicine and health, as well as a lunch-and-learn for students interested in the arts,” Hildebrand said. “November will begin lunch-and-learns with military recruiters for students interested in exploring careers in all branches of the military.”
 Advisers in each school also have escorted students to two college and career fairs and are starting to schedule and place juniors and seniors into job-shadow opportunities across the city.
 At Jefferson, dozens of students completed four-hour job shadows that immersed them in everything from architecture and banking to auto mechanics. Other professionals came into the schools to meet with students, and there were small-group industry tours lined up at places such as Citibank and the law enforcement training center.
 Each branch of the military did a lunch-and-learn to explain occupations in the armed services to students.
 At Washington High School, where the college and career advisers are new this year, “I love that they’re bringing back job shadowing and internships,” principal Kari Papke said.
 “What a great opportunity for our business partners to come alongside kids and say, ‘Why don’t you come see what this looks like?’ Connections matter. It helps kids see what’s actually needed. And sometimes, you realize it’s not what you wanted to do, or you absolutely love it. I just love the partnerships that it has the potential to create between our local community and our schools.”
 At Washington, “they started with a focus on seniors because those are the kids where we have limited time left with them,” Papke said. “We have a lot of kids meeting with our college and career advisers … so they’re already very busy and working with a lot of kids, which is great.”
 There’s a correlation between how many students at a school are eligible for free and reduced lunch and what percentage go on to further education, she added.
 “Which also just shows you those are the students who sometimes need a little more support,” Papke said. “There are more barriers to knock down.”
 College and career advisers also don’t leave a student’s side after graduation. They continue to focus on college retention, especially for low-income students who might be more easily inclined to leave for the workforce.
 “A student has to complete the FAFSA every year, so when they leave high school and we’ve given the support, they might not understand they can go to to their financial aid office and get that support,” Hildebrand said. “Kids might not understand the mental health resources, the tutoring resources, and we will be familiar with the resources, and we’ve built a relationship with them, so we want to keep the relationship going and give additional support as they head off on their own.”
 Funding the $1 million effort “wasn’t as hard as I thought it was going to be,” he added, while acknowledging that repeating the fundraising annually could be a challenge. Seven donors gave $50,000 or more in annual commitments, and the South Dakota Community Foundation gave a $100,000 grant.
 “When you sit down with a prospective donor and explain what you’re doing, there’s a lot of understanding it’s an important program,” Hildebrand said. “My hope is someday the school district will bring it into their funding once they see the proof of what this team can do and make these permanent positions.”
 College and career advisers are available to all students, though emphasis is placed on first-generation postsecondary students, students with diverse backgrounds and students from low-income households. They tend to face the biggest barriers to college or tech school, Hildebrand said.
 “It doesn’t matter how long it takes to help a student if you got them across the finish line,” he said. “That’s what we’re here for. Helping them find a way to go with minimal debt is life-changing, and our team is really well trained to help any student go through this process.”
